articles.headline: Why you should never reply with STOP when you receive spam texts
keyFacts: Replying STOP to spam texts from unknown scammers confirms your number is active and can lead to receiving more junk messages.
Users should only reply STOP to legitimate alerts they signed up for and instead use device tools to report or block spam.
Smartphone owners can reduce spam by adjusting filter settings in iOS or Android, forwarding messages to 7726, or using carrier protections.
body: Why you should never reply with STOP when you receive spam texts
An honest opt-out method for marketing messages sends a different signal to shady scammers.

You've likely noticed the "STOP to cancel" note when you receive texts from short codes. And for legitimate communications that you asked to receive from restaurants, surveys, loyalty programs and similar, STOP is a fine way to cut them off. But it's not your only option for ending unwanted texts, and for many kinds, it can do more harm than good.

Nobody wants garbage texts about phony job offers, illicit encounters or other scams, but it's important to think carefully about how you respond to them. Rather than deleting them and dealing with more in the future, you have other options — and they're ones that won't prompt more incoming junk.

Remember to treat any messages from unknown numbers with caution, since they're used for "wrong number" scams and all kinds of other schemes. Don't tap an unexpected link, even if it claims you have an unpaid toll or need to confirm details to fix a delivery problem.
The issue with replying STOP

Marketing texts from actual businesses include the "STOP to end" line because they're legally required to give you a way out, similar to the mandatory Unsubscribe link at the bottom of emails. This is covered by the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA). In those cases, after replying STOP, you shouldn't hear from them again, but they do legally have 10 business days to stop messages to your number.

However, not all the texts you get from unknown numbers are like this. Spam texts that advertise lonely singles, too-good-to-be-true job offers, package delivery scams or other types of nonsense aren't operating within normal marketing laws. You might thus reply STOP out of habit, even if they don't include a note about that.

By doing so, you're confirming to the sender that your number is active, which will likely result in you getting even more junk texts. It costs spammers almost nothing to send out many thousands of texts to random numbers, but few of those are confirmed as live, so you're making yourself a target. Replying can also demonstrate that you aren't able to recognize a text scam, possibly tagging you for future efforts if they think they can hook you.
How to deal with scam texts

Only reply STOP when you want to stop getting alerts you specifically signed up for. For anything else, never respond; instead, you should use your phone's tools to deal with unwanted messages safely.

On iPhone, you should see a Stop or Report Spam button under messages from unknown senders that include a STOP note. Tap this, and you can choose Delete and Stop or Delete and Report Spam. Both erase the conversation from your phone; the former sends a STOP reply after doing this, while the latter reports the message to your carrier and Apple. For messages without a mention of STOP, the only option is Report Spam.

A similar option appears at the bottom of conversations with unknown senders; tap Delete followed by Delete and Report Spam. In case the number keeps contacting you, tap the number at the top of the conversation and choose Block Contact to cut off all communication.

On Android, you can report an entire conversation as spam in Google Messages by holding it in the list, then choosing Block > Report spam. Alternatively, open a conversation, tap the three-dot More button, then choose Details > Block & report spam. You'll also have the option to block the number.

For either platform, you can also long-press the message and forward it to 7726 (SPAM on a keypad). This reports the text to your carrier for analysis, helping it block spammers across the network. You might get a response asking for the sender's number, so wait to block it until you've confirmed this.
Fighting back against spam messages

Even when you know what to do upon receiving junk texts, it's better if you don't get them in the first place. Android and iOS both have ways to filter low-quality messages so you aren't getting alerted for nothing.

If you have an iPhone, visit Settings > Apps > Messages, where you have a few choices. Turn on Filter Spam to send obvious garbage to a separate Spam folder. Enable Screen Unknown Senders, then messages from numbers not in your contacts will go to their own folder. And under Text Message Filter, enable the built-in Text Message Filter to put other texts into groups like Transactions and Promotions.

The Allow Notifications menu controls which of these groups send you alerts. Some third-party iPhone apps offer their own message filtering options, which will appear here. Once it's all set up, access the filtered groups from the three-line Filter button at the top-right corner of Messages.

On Android, open Google Messages, tap your profile picture at the top-right corner and choose Messages settings. Choose Protection & Safety, then you can choose from Standard protection or Enhanced protection for junk messages. In your profile picture menu, choose Spam & blocked to review filtered messages.
Other anti-spam options

Many mobile carriers offer their own protections from spam messages (like T-Mobile ScamShield), which are worth a look if you're still receiving trash. Depending on your carrier, you might activate this by changing a toggle in your account, dialing a code to activate or installing a separate app. The base features should be free; it's almost certainly not worth paying for any premium subscriptions on offer. Third-party tools like Truecaller are another option.

Otherwise, be careful of where you give out your number. While spammers often get your number from leaks, other times your contact details spread around when you sign up on a shady website or a company sells them. When making a new account, always check the settings to see if you can limit your information from being shared for marketing purposes. That can help stop spam calls as well as texts.

articles.headline: Blue Jays land Japanese star after missing out on Teruaki Sato
keyFacts: The Toronto Blue Jays missed out on free agents Teruaki Sato and Trevor Rogers after both reportedly agreed to deals with the Chicago Cubs.
Jon Heyman reported the Blue Jays agreed to a five-year, $80 million contract with Japanese pitcher Kaima Taira.
Taira, a 27-year-old right-hander who posted a 1.36 ERA in Japan last season, will join Toronto's starting rotation.
body: The Toronto Blue Jays were one of many teams involved in the Teruaki Sato sweepstakes this MLB offseason. But on Tuesday morning, the Chicago Cubs reportedly agreed with Sato on a $120 million contract over six years.

But that wasn't all the bad news for the Blue Jays from the Cubs. Trevor Rogers also reportedly joined the Cubs, and he was the next-best left-handed starter available this offseason. He would've been a great fallback option after missing out on Tarik Skubal.

However, the Blue Jays have made a big roster move. According to Jon Heyman of The New York Post, the Blue Jays have agreed to terms with Japanese star pitcher Kaima Taira on a five-year, $80 million contract.
Blue Jays to sign Kaima Taira to $80M contract after missing out on Sato, Rogers
"BREAKING: Kaima Taira to the Jays. $80 million /5 years. Opt out after year 3," Heyman reported Tuesday.
This is some big news for the Blue Jays, as following missing out on Sato and Rogers, they've landed a big-name free agent this Fall in Taira.
Taira is a 27-year-old right-handed pitcher who was a star overseas in Japan as a starting pitcher. This past season, in 23 starts across 146 innings of work, Taira posted an incredible 1.36 ERA.
He went 12-5 on the season, and struck out 141 batters while walking 45 and allowing just four home runs all season long.
The Blue Jays are adding Taira to their rotation, pairing him with Dylan Cease, Jose Soriano, Trey Yesavage, and Coy Ponce.

While Toronto missed out on Sato, arguably the best outfielder, and Rogers, arguably the best non-Skubal left-handed starter, they've landed star Japanese pitcher Kaima Taira on a five-year, $80 million deal that has an opt-out after the third season.

articles.headline: Texas Democrats add high-speed rail to ‘Californication’ project
keyFacts: Texas Democrats proposed high-speed passenger rail lines connecting major cities such as Austin, San Antonio, Waco, and Dallas.
A feasibility study estimated the potential cost for the Austin-to-San Antonio rail connection alone at $13.5 billion.
Republicans kept their Texas state Senate majority, allowing them to oppose legislation from the newly elected Democratic state House majority.
body: In our recent column on the broken “blue” model of governance, we revisited the endless, cartoonish failure that is California ’s high-speed rail debacle. In short, a train project to connect San Francisco and Los Angeles was approved by Golden State voters back in 2008. The work was to be completed by 2020 at a price tag of approximately $33 billion.

Eighteen years later, and six years after the original deadline, zero active track has been laid. The intended destinations have shifted from Los Angeles and San Francisco to the outskirts of minor regional cities, and even those places may not be connected until at least 2040, if ever. The estimated cost of this fiasco has roughly quadrupled, with some projections ballooning even more.

It’s a disgrace. And to anyone whose hard-earned tax dollars have not been set ablaze in pursuit of this boondoggle, it’s a punchline about the wasteful incompetence and dysfunction of California’s sputtering experiment in government supremacy.
Apparently, however, some newly empowered Democrats in Texas have decided it would be a fine idea to emulate their West Coast counterparts not only in general but specifically on this:
“Democrats who helped turn Texas blue are already pitching a familiar California-style idea in the Lone Star State: a high-speed rail line connecting some of its biggest cities.

Austin City Council Member Vanessa Fuentes and San Antonio City Council Member Jalen McKee-Rodriguez are pushing for a passenger rail connection between the two cities, arguing that a changing political landscape presents an opportunity to finally get trains moving in Texas. And state Rep. John Bucy, a Democrat representing Austin, has introduced legislation that would pave the way for a much bigger project connecting Dallas, Waco, Austin and San Antonio along the Interstate 35 corridor…

The proposal comes with a staggering potential price tag of $13.5 billion for the Austin-to-San Antonio connection alone, according to a recent feasibility study. … ‘It’s time for trains in Texas,’ the two city council members declared in a social media video promoting the idea. But the ambitious pitch may sound familiar to Californians, who have spent nearly two decades watching their own bullet train project balloon in cost and fall further behind schedule.”

Texas’s newly elected Democrats haven’t even taken power, yet their rapacious coalition is already brainstorming ways to squander the state’s responsibly established and carefully maintained emergency “rainy day” fund and blow open the budget.

It is almost unfathomable that they’d instantly gravitate toward replicating one of the most glaring and high-profile Democratic governing failures in the whole country, but some of them have done just that.

Two factors that might make a Lone Star version of California’s misadventure less disastrous are (1) the state’s finances being in very good shape, no thanks at all to Democrats, and (2) the state lacking California’s nightmarish tapestry of bureaucracy, regulations, and special interests. In short, people can still actually build things in Texas — for now, and again, no thanks to Democrats.

Those two advantages exist because Democrats have lacked the power to run the place into the ground, as they have in California for decades. Texas voters may have chosen to send a message to Republicans several weeks ago, but it’s unclear how many of them truly intended to sign up for what’s coming.
MAMDANI’S STARTLING OMISSION

Democrats swept the statewide races and gained more than 20 seats in the state House to claim a lower chamber majority. The saving grace for the GOP — and it still feels a bit surreal that Republicans need any sort of governing firewall in Texas — is that not a single state Senate seat changed hands this cycle, keeping that red majority firmly in place.

Its members will have to use their power to prevent a lot of damage over the next two years, at which time voters (including many who sat at home this year) must decide whether this purplish-blue hue is an unusual interlude and outlier or a new normal.

body: Sen. Deb Fischer , R-Neb., announced Monday that her husband, Bruce Fischer, died over the weekend.

"It is with a heavy heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Bruce," Fischer said in a statement posted on X. "Bruce was my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family. His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him."
"On November 22, Bruce passed away peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors," the statement continued.

"Our family is heartbroken by his passing, but we find comfort in the life we shared with him. I will cherish the decades we spent building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills. Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher."

articles.headline: MLB rumors: Corey Seager willing to waive his NTC for Phili, plus latest on Mets, Tigers, Guardians, more
keyFacts: Texas Rangers shortstop Corey Seager is willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Philadelphia Phillies, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports.
The Cleveland Guardians agreed to a one-year, $17.5 million free-agent contract with left-hander Kris Bubic, according to reports.
The Detroit Tigers agreed to a one-year, $5 million free-agent contract with infielder Ha-Seong Kim, ESPN reports.
body: The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples. Just recently, for instance, the New York Mets landed the biggest fish in the pond by signing ace Tarik Skubal to a record contract. Not long after, the Chicago Cubs fortified their rotation with Trevor Rogers and their outfield with Teruaki Sato, and Freddy Peralta is headed to the Baltimore Orioles. More's surely to come before lockout day arrives.
Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Tuesday's supply just below.
Corey Seager willing to waive no-trade clause to join Phillies

The Philadelphia Phillies are open to moving Trea Turner off of shortstop given that he's now a pronounced defensive liability. Speaking of openness, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phillies and upgrade the position for them, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports.

Now 32, Seager will always have health and durability concerns, but he remains a plus defensive shortstop who produces well at the plate by positional standards. Signed to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season (just before the last lockout, in fact), Seager is owed another $155 million through the 2031 season. The Rangers are reportedly looking to shake things up. The Phillies, meantime, are trying to keep their contention window open. It's a fit both ways, at least in theory. Such a move would likely mean a move to the outfield for Turner, who himself has very little trade value thanks to his ongoing decline and big contract.
Guardians land Bubic

The Cleveland Guardians have agreed to a free-agent contract with left-hander Kris Bubic, Sportsnet reports. The contract is for $17.5 million over one year, according to ESPN. Bubic, 29, made nine starts for the Kansas City Royals last season, and after the trade to the Los Angeles Dodgers, he was used out of the bullpen. Bubic has an outlier fastball thanks to its rise and his unusual release point, and he's an interesting "ceiling" candidate in the rotation. However, his substantial history of injuries may mean he's best used out of the bullpen.
Tigers add Kim

The Detroit Tigers have added infield depth by agreeing to terms with Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year, $5 million free agent contract, ESPN reports. Kim, 31, is coming off a rough partial season with the Atlanta Braves, but he has a more palatable OPS+ of 91 for his career. He's been a primary shortstop in recent years and also has significant time spent at second base and third base.
Twins still looking for help on the market

Even after achieving a reunion with veteran starting pitcher Sonny Gray, the Minnesota Twins are still looking to fortify their roster for a return to contention in 2027. The club still hopes to make one more significant addition this offseason and add another player who may not grab as many headlines, the Athletic reports. Atop the wishlist are a first baseman or a second baseman and another lefty reliever.
Mets may be eyeing more rotation additions

Even after the splash addition of Skubal, the Mets may not be done adding starting pitchers in the service of a rebound season in 2027. On that front, the Mets may be interested in adding a starting pitcher on a short-term deal for next season, the Athletic reports. That would likely limit them to the back half of the market, especially with so many bigger names reaching agreements.

articles.headline: US House counsel denies backing controversial raid on Ilhan Omar’s home
keyFacts: House General Counsel Matthew Berry denied federal prosecutors' court claims that his office supported an October 12 raid on Representative Ilhan Omar's home.
A judge rejected federal prosecutors' assertions and ruled Representative Ilhan Omar must be allowed to assert constitutional privilege over seized items.
The Trump administration is investigating Omar over alleged immigration fraud, with top officials calling for her deportation and loss of citizenship.
body: Washington, DC, United States – The US House’s general counsel has accused federal prosecutors of wrongly claiming in court that the chamber’s legal office backed a raid on the home of Representative Ilhan Omar.

Court documents unsealed on Monday evening show that in the lead-up to the early morning October 12 raid on Omar’s home in Washington, DC, US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh ordered the Department of Justice to give the lawmaker an opportunity to assert that some materials taken by them are constitutionally protected because she is a sitting member of Congress.

Matthew Berry, the House’s top lawyer, was tasked with helping protect that constitutional separation of powers for lawmakers, under a provision of the Constitution referred to as the Speech or Debate clause.

At court before the raid on Omar’s house, the Justice Department alleged it had consulted Berry and received his backing. Federal prosecutors told the court that Berry’s office “refused to be involved in the search” and that, “echoing the United States’ position, explained that, in his view, Speech or Debate clause protections do not extend to a member’s private residence”.
Berry told Al Jazeera that the Justice Department’s claim that his refusal to be involved in the search meant he agreed with the department was “categorically false”.

Berry acknowledged that his office had responded to a Justice Department email on the eve of the raid, saying that his office would not be present during the operation itself, but pointed out that a court had ruled Omar’s representatives must be given the chance to assert the constitutional privilege over which items were taken from her home.

“The Department of Justice’s assertion that I refused to be involved in the search of Representative Ilhan Omar’s residence because I agreed with the Department that Speech or Debate Clause protections do not extend to a Member’s private residence is categorically false,” Berry said in a statement.

According to court documents, Judge Sharbaugh rejected federal prosecutors’ assertions that the key constitutional provision shielding lawmakers from turning over work-related materials did not apply to Omar’s home, saying “this court sees differently.”
‘Unlawful search’
The raid on Omar’s home was widely condemned by Democratic lawmakers, who said it was a dangerous intrusion by President Donald Trump that violated constitutional separation of powers.

Omar’s lawyers, in a letter to the Justice Department after the raid in October, had said, “This search was neither justified nor lawful.” They said investigators did not provide them with a copy of the warrant in advance, and seized her phone and passport, along with other materials from her home.
Omar’s office did not respond to a request for comment from Al Jazeera.

A federal raid on a sitting member of Congress’ home was “extremely unusual”, and it would be highly doubtful the House Office of General Counsel would not want to be involved, said Timothy Heaphy, a former federal prosecutor who served as lead counsel for the House committee that investigated the January 6, 2021 attacks on the US Capitol.

The House general counsel’s office “represents the institutional prerogatives of the House. If a committee subpoenas something and there is an objection, the House’s General Counsel litigates that … if there is a Speech and Debate issue, they generally are involved,” Heaphy said.
“They would certainly want a voice in protecting the Speech and Debate privilege for members, regardless of politics. They are supposed to be bipartisan.”
The administration of US President Donald Trump is investigating Omar over alleged immigration fraud, with the president and top officials calling for her to lose her US citizenship and be deported.

Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.

articles.headline: Bare fist, megastructure climbing roguelike White Knuckle gets its penultimate region in The Core, a sterile, hostile reactor sector that you'll probably die in
keyFacts: The early access roguelike White Knuckle added its sixth and penultimate region, a hostile reactor sector called The Core.
Players can now use a new major artifact called The Scissors to gain a spectral form and increased combat abilities.
The update introduces new weapons, perks, and room tiles to the game, with one final region planned for the future.
body: The beauty of stepping into a digital world is that it allows me to accomplish things I couldn't possibly dream of doing in the real one, like, say, climbing anything that's higher than your average step ladder. White Knuckle is one such game that's all about playing around with uncomfortable heights, and a new update for the early access roguelike went live this week introducing a new, hostile environment: The Core.

The sixth region to be added to the game, and the "penultimate challenge," implying that there's just one more area to come after this one, The Core takes you to Habitation Blue's reactor sector. "Use everything you have available to fight through the now Mass-controlled Superstructure Automated Processing System (SAPS) and her array of mechanized defenses," explains a Steam news post. "The Core is the sterile power station of the Superstructure, a massive network of coolant lines, offices, catwalks, and more, all of which is highly secured by an army of turrets, drones, and androids. Even without the Mass hot on your tail it would not be easy to escape."

There are a few new subregions to be found too, of course, but more importantly a new major artifact. It's called The Scissors, and with it you cut off your hands ("yes, really") to "gain a spectral form that increases your reach, hand stamina, and damage," while using the artifact. You can also throw the scissors like a boomerang to hurt enemies from afar, and "killing enemies also counts as eating if using Survival Mode binding, or the perks Conditioned Polyphagia & Unstoppable Conviction."

Beyond this there's a selection of new weapons, like the piton crossbow which shoots "pitons at range, to set up routes and to deal extreme damage." The pulse pump is a new trinket that introduces a chargeable mid-air jump. There's new perks like one called nest egg, where you gain a "second major artifact at the start of the Nest, at the cost of halving all roach deposits in your run." Previous regions have also received some new room tiles, and there's a few fresh cosmetics to pick up too. There's some secret thing to find in this update as well, "but you'll need to play to find out…" Hop to it, I guess!

articles.headline: MLB Hot Stove tracker: Live updates on latest news, rumors, signings and trades in 2026 free agency
keyFacts: A lockout is scheduled to begin on December 1, which will halt all MLB player transactions until a new collective bargaining agreement is reached.
The New York Mets signed free agent pitcher Tarik Skubal to a nine-year, $450 million contract, making him the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history.
Multiple teams are completing signings and trades before the deadline, including the Cubs adding Teruki Sato and Trevor Rogers to their roster.
body: The heart of the MLB offseason is typically the first two weeks of December, but this isn't a typical offseason.

A lockout is set to take effect at the end of the day on Dec. 1, ending all transactions until the owners and players agree to a new collective bargaining agreement. As we saw five years ago, that will likely take some time.

2021 offers an indication of how offseason transactions could play out: there was a flurry of activity leading up to start of the lockout, but plenty of significant moves had to wait until after the lockout was lifted more than three months later.
If reports are any indication, though, No. 1 free agent Tarik Skubal has a strong chance to sign before the lockout begins, raising the level of intrigue around free agency.
The Sporting News is tracking the latest MLB rumors, signings and trades before the lockout begins. Follow along below with the latest news.

articles.headline: Plaud's pocket-sized Note Pro AI voice recorder is built for the moments you miss in meetings — now at its lowest ever price
keyFacts: The Plaud Note Pro voice recorder has dropped to its lowest Amazon price of $150 for Black Friday.
The pocket-sized device uses AI to generate transcripts, summaries, and action points from recordings in over 100 languages.
Users must upgrade to a paid Pro plan to record more conversations beyond the included 300 monthly minutes.
body: We've had some excellent experiences with Plaud's line of business voice recorders - they turned our reviewer from transcription sceptic to die-hard fan.
So, I was pleased to see that the Plaud Note Pro has dropped to its lowest ever price of $150 (was $189) at Amazon for Black Friday.
The Plaud Note Pro can save you loads of time by recording notes from your meetings and interviews - so you get all of the detail you need without the pain of manual transcription.

The pocket-sized Plaud Note Pro measures just 0.12 inches, weighing in at 1.06 oz. The package includes the transcription device, a magnetic case and ring, charging cable, and a free Starter Plan with 300 transcription minutes per month.
Why we recommend the Plaud Note Pro

This slim, 30g recorder attaches magnetically to your smartphone and captures meetings, interviews, and phone calls. It’s got four microphones, it comes with 64GB of storage, and it’s got a built-in AMOLED display - so it represents an impressive next step when compared to the original Plaud Note device.
Once recordings are transferred to the Plaud app, its AI can produce transcripts, summaries, meeting minutes, action points, and mind maps based on your conversations.
The app supports over 100 languages, and if you switch to endurance recording mode, you should get 50 hours of battery life from the Note Pro.

We awarded the original Plaud Note 5 stars in our review, praising its simple operation and impressive transcription and summarisation. Bear in mind, though, that you’ll need to upgrade to a Pro plan if you want to record more meetings.
Price context and history
This is the lowest price the Plaud Note Pro has been at Amazon - beating a previous low of $160. So, a genuine Black Friday deal here, and a worthwhile discount on a useful productivity tool.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy it if… you want to accelerate how quickly you get transcripts and notes from your meetings
❌ Skip it if… you don’t want to pay an ongoing subscription cost or you don’t need to record many conversations

articles.headline: GTA 6 Data Reveals Only 40% of Players Have Cleared Chapter 2
keyFacts: Data from PSNProfiles and TrueAchievements shows that only about 40% of PlayStation 5 players and 31% of Xbox players have completed Chapter 2.
Despite high player engagement and average playtimes exceeding 17 hours on PS5, few users have progressed past the game's third chapter.
Take-Two Interactive reported that GTA 6 set a new entertainment industry record with 32.5 million copies sold during its pre-release period.
body: If your feed is full of reassurance: most players aren’t as far along as you probably think.

According to PSNProfiles, only 66.22% of Grand Theft Auto 6 players on PlayStation 5 have earned the trophy for completing Chapter 1, which takes place in the Leonida Keys. The numbers on Xbox are similar, with 56% of players having beaten that part of the game, according to TrueAchievements. This completion percentage feels particularly significant because the first chapter of the game is a big departure from classic GTA, with Jason living out a relatively low-key existence interrupted by the occasional shootout with backwoods drug dealers. Still, it seems a solid chunk of players are more than happy fishing with Cal for now.

Meanwhile, only 40.55% of players have cleared Chapter 2 on PS5, and 31% on Xbox. Again, considering that Chapter 3 is arguably where the game becomes more of a traditional Grand Theft Auto entry, as you officially enter Vice City, it’s a bit of a surprise that the numbers are so low, even if it takes close to 20 hours to get there.

As for the rest of the game, few have gotten past Chapter 3: 6.45% have cleared that chapter on PS5, compared to 4% on Xbox; 1.26% have cleared Chapter 4 on PS5 against 1% on Xbox; and a tiny 0.88% have cleared the final mission on PlayStation against fewer than 1% on Xbox.

Although it’s tempting to assume these low completion numbers are simply because the game came out so recently, Sony released player engagement numbers that made it clear most have already put a ton of time into GTA 6. Mat Piscatella, senior director at market research firm Circana, revealed that players spent an average of more than 8 hours playing the game on launch day. As of Nov. 23, PS5 players had already spent an average of 17.4 hours playing. While users are playing a lot and sticking with the game, most are taking their time. Rockstar previously said the main story takes around 50 hours to finish.
An historic launch

Shortly after GTA 6 was released, publisher Take-Two Interactive announced that the game had set a “new record for entertainment across any medium,” making it the biggest launch in entertainment history. It sold 32.5 million copies during its pre-release period, generating $3.79 billion in revenue. In the previously mentioned post that announced PlayStation engagement numbers, Sony also said GTA 6 was the biggest launch in PlayStation history and that 39 million people had played it on the PS5 as of Monday.

articles.headline: China places Shanghai CCP leader under investigation for corruption as Xi expands purge
keyFacts: Chinese state media reported that Shanghai Communist Party Secretary Chen Jining is under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and law.
Chen has overseen Shanghai since 2022, making him one of the highest-ranking political leaders targeted in President Xi Jinping's expanding purge.
The ongoing crackdown has also significantly reduced China's Central Military Commission leadership and removed dozens of senior military officers.
body: Shanghai Communist Party Secretary Chen Jining is under investigation for suspected violations of party discipline and law, Chinese state media reported Tuesday, adding another senior official to President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge of China’s political and military leadership.

The announcements from Xinhua News Agency and China Central Television offered few details about the investigation, saying only that Chen was “suspected of serious violations of discipline and law.” Authorities did not identify specific allegations against him or indicate what consequences he could face.

Chen has served as Shanghai’s top Communist Party official since 2022, overseeing China’s largest city and one of its most important economic and financial centers. Before taking the post, he held senior positions in Beijing’s municipal government and served as China’s environmental protection minister.

Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai, attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People’s Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. (AP Photo/Ng Han Guan, File)

His investigation comes amid an extensive shake-up of the country’s senior leadership, with Xi’s anti-corruption campaign increasingly reaching officials at the highest levels of the party and military.

Among those previously caught up in the purge are Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, the body responsible for overseeing China’s armed forces. Ma Xingrui, a former provincial party secretary and another member of the country’s senior political leadership, has also been removed.

The scale of the crackdown has been particularly striking within the military. The Central Military Commission, which had seven members when Xi began his third term, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who has overseen investigations into fellow military officials.
THE GOP KNIVES ARE OUT FOR TRUMP COMMERCE SECRETARY HOWARD LUTNICK

The removals have not been limited to the commission’s top ranks. As many as 33 officers at the theater-command level, one tier below the commission, have also been dismissed, according to research tracking the military shake-up.

Xi has made his anti-corruption drive a defining feature of his leadership, presenting it as a way to eliminate misconduct, strengthen party discipline, and ensure loyalty throughout the government and armed forces. The campaign has also given him an increasingly powerful role in determining who remains in China’s senior leadership.

articles.headline: Iran developing chemical weapons, Israeli defense minister says
keyFacts: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said Iran is developing chemical weapons and warned Israel may launch a preemptive strike to thwart the threat.
Iran's army commander said the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed to unauthorized traffic, while U.S. officials reported rising oil shipments.
Saudi Arabian authorities said 11 people were injured on Tuesday after Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Saudi Arabian authorities said 11 people were injured Tuesday in a strike by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels that hit a tower in Riyadh's Financial District. Yemen's civil war has intensified since the summer, with the Iranian proxy group threatening to choke off oil and gas shipments from Saudi Arabia.

- Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them. Iran has repeatedly denied they are developing chemical weapons.

- The commander of Iran's army reiterated on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is closed to all unauthorized traffic and will remain closed until Iran's seven conditions are met, and he appeared to call for Iranian forces to step up their attacks on commercial ships in the vital waterway.
Oil tanker traffic through Strait of Hormuz continues to rise, U.S. officials say
As Brent crude continues to hover around $90, its lowest level since late August, the U.S. continues to increase the amount of oil it is bringing out from the Persian Gulf.

Despite the number of attacks on tankers attempting to pass through the strait reaching their highest level in October — and with November already on pace to exceed that number — U.S. officials insist substantial oil is getting through.

"Last week was a notable one for tankers. More than 108 million barrels of crude oil were shipped through the strait by Gulf partners with U.S. protection, the largest weekly volume to date," U.S. Central Command spokesman Tim Hawkins said, referring to the date of the start of the conflict in February.

Since declaration of a ceasefire on April 7, more than 8,000 commercial vessels have transited the strait — about half under U.S. protection, according to a U.S. official. The official said more than 95% of ships are passing through the strait without any issue.
Iran developing chemical weapons, Israeli defense minister says, warns of possible preemptive strike
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."
In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."
The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.
CBS/AFP
Iranian singer lashed for "outraging public decency" becomes "a symbol of resistance"

Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without the head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.

Ahmadi was dealt the corporal punishment for her chosen attire during a livestreamed concert in 2024, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Emtemad on Monday. But Iranian women who spoke with CBS News on Tuesday said she was punished not for breaking the rule, but for daring to publicly defy the country's repressive regime — defiance that has made her "a symbol of resistance."

Ahmadi's lawyer told Emtemad that the singer and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom, as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
Iran army chief says Strait of Hormuz "must become increasingly closed day by day"

The commander of Iran's army reiterated the regime's stance on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is closed to all unauthorized traffic and will remain closed until are met, and he appeared to call for Iranian forces to step up their attacks on commercial ships in the vital waterway.

Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said during an event attended by senior army commanders that Iran "did not allow the enemy to impose the pain of war solely on the Iranian people, but rather the warmongers have also felt the pain of war at their gas stations and in their living rooms."
In his remarks, carried by Iranian state television network IRIB, Hatami called on the Iranian Navy commander to make conditions in the waterway "more difficult."

"Until the Islamic Republic of Iran's seven conditions are met, not only will the Strait of Hormuz remain closed, but it must become increasingly closed day by day," he said. "Conditions must become more difficult for the enemy, and stronger control must be exercised over it."
11 injured in Houthi attack on Riyadh financial district tower, Saudi authorities say
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense agency said a strike by Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen on a building in Riyadh's Financial District left 11 people injured on Tuesday.
The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepalese nationals and four Egyptian nationals, according to the agency.

The Yemeni rebels did not immediately issue any statement about the attack, but late last week they issued a "warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries."
Iranian general says U.S. forces will "remain within range of Iran's armed forces" even if relocated

The Chief of the General Staff of Iran's armed forces said Tuesday that the Islamic Republic would continue targeting U.S. forces wherever they are, even if they are moved from damaged bases in the Middle East to "more distant areas."

Major General Ali Abdollahi, in remarks carried by Iranian state television network IRIB, claimed U.S. bases across the region had sustained "severe damage" due to Iranian attacks, "and a considerable number of them were rendered inoperable."

"Any relocation of US bases in the region will not change the Islamic Republic of Iran's resolve to confront threats," Abdollahi said Tuesday. "Wherever these bases are stationed, they will remain within range of Iran's armed forces if necessary."
Photos in September revealed for the first time the widespread damage and destruction caused by Iranian attacks to buildings and vehicles at multiple U.S. positions across the Middle East.
The Defense Department's inspector a fresh report in September on the war that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft.
Saudis say tower in Riyadh financial district hit in "terrorist attack" after Houthi threat

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels confirmed an attack on a tower in the kingdom's financial district Tuesday, after witnesses reported the capital's tallest skyscraper being hit.

"One of the towers in the financial center was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack. The relevant authorities are currently inspecting the attack site," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a social media post.
The Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district late last week days after Saudi authorities accused the rebels of damaging a different skyscraper in the district with a previous strike.

"We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries," Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree wrote in a Telegram post on Friday. "Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Global oil prices drop below $90, continuing slow decline despite ongoing attacks on ships in Gulf

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, was trading below $90 a barrel Tuesday morning, near its lowest point since late August. Global oil prices have been on a downward trend since late October after hitting a peak over the summer near $120 per barrel.

The drop comes despite ongoing attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz, both by Iran targeting vessels it accuses of violating its restrictions on the waterway, and by the U.S. military as it enforces its blockade of Iranian ports.

Iran's threat to commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf region — which it has wielded as a weapon since the U.S. and Israel launched their joint war on the country — severely restricted global oil supplies for much of the conflict.

Since major hostilities eased over the summer, oil prices have eased — likely as independent monitors say the flow of oil from Gulf producers has increased steadily. The International Energy Agency says crude exports from the Gulf have recovered to about 74% of pre-war levels, and the agency expects oil market surpluses within months.
The rebound in supplies appears to be offsetting market concerns over Iran's ongoing attacks and threats to ships, and President Trump's repeated threats to renew U.S. strikes against Iran.
Value of Iranian currency plunges on black market after new sanctions announced
Iran's currency plunged on the black market Tuesday after the U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions.

The Treasury announced sanctions Monday against more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, alleged front companies and individuals said to be part of the country's "shadow banking" network. It said the network was "overseen" by Iran's central bank.
By Tuesday afternoon, the U.S. dollar was trading at around 2.82 million rials, up about 5% from around 2.68 million the day before, according to websites monitoring black market rates.

"While Iran's shadow banking system moves the funds generated by Iran's international trade, the Iran Center for Exchange plays matchmaker and guides these funds to their ultimate destination inside Iran," OFAC said.
Houthis accuse Saudi forces of killing 30 thoroughbred horses with airstrike on stable
A news outlet run by Iran's Houthi rebel allies accused Saudi forces on Tuesday of killing 30 thoroughbred horses with a strike that hit a stable in Yemen.

Al-Masirah TV, which is owned by the Houthis, said Saudi aircraft conducted strikes in Sanaa and Amran that targeted civilian properties. Al-Masirah labelled the strike as a Saudi crime and said the horses held material and sentimental value.

The Houthis have been locked in grueling, more than decade-long civil war against Yemen's government forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. Recent Houthi gains have consolidated the group's control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which the group has tried to use to disrupt Saudi oil exports.
In a separate report, Al-Misarah said 1,421 civilians have been killed by Saudi strikes in Yemen since Sept. 2, citing the Houthi-controlled Yemeni Ministry of Health and Environment.
Rubio meets Qatari leader in Washington

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with the Prime Minister of Qatar Monday in Washington - a regularly scheduled biannual meeting with a close Persian Gulf ally that comes as the tiny nation continues efforts to broker a deal between the U.S. and Iran.
Qatar, like most other U.S. Gulf allies, has faced attacks during the war by Iran, which has continued to threaten any country that supports American military operations.

The Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement Tuesday that Rubio had "reaffirmed the United States' commitment to Qatar's security," and underscored "the importance of the defense partnership in strengthening joint capabilities and protecting shared interests."

"On behalf of President Trump, Secretary Rubio expressed gratitude to His Highness the Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and the government of the State of Qatar for their leadership as a global mediator and close partner in advancing peace, stability, and security worldwide," the Qatari Foreign Ministry statement said.
Multiple ships reportedly struck near Strait of Hormuz

The British navy's maritime monitoring agency confirmed on Tuesday an attack on a tanker the previous day near the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran issued new claims of commercial vessels trying to use the vital waterway without its permission hitting sea mines.

The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said a ship was anchored off the coast of the United Arab Emirates on Monday and that "a fire was reported onboard the vessel but no casualties have been reported at this time."
Meanwhile, the Iranian navy said two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines east of the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
The navy said the ship entered the strait "after disabling their identification and navigation systems."
Iran has previously struck ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz which it considers to be transiting without their permission.

The Iranian Navy said in a statement the waterway "will never be reopened until Iran's objectives and demands are met, and oil tanker owners are required to coordinate with the armed forces to ensure safe passage through this strategic strait."
U.S. reportedly investigating cyberattacks on oil tankers

The U.S. is investigating whether Iran is involved in cyberattacks targeting dozens of ships carrying oil and other explosive substances, according to sources familiar with the matter quoted by the Wall Street Journal.

As many as 50 ships carrying oil, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, the Journal reported, citing the sources. In some cases, ships have also received bomb threats.
According to the sources, Iran is the primary suspect of the incidents, while Russia is also seen as a possible culprit.
The Journal had previously reported two of the cyberattacks targeted ships heading to Texas in September.
Houthi media says 25 killed or missing after Saudi strikes
Houthi-affiliated news agency Saba said Tuesday that a Saudi strike on buses and trucks had left 25 people dead or missing in Yemen's southwest.
The Iran-backed fighters, who control swathes of Yemen, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognised government.

"The toll from the Saudi enemy planes' targeting of buses and trucks in Wadi Mabaq, Lahj Governorate, has risen to 25 martyrs or missing, and six wounded," reported the Houthi-run Saba news agency, adding that the continued presence of Saudi aircraft over the area was hindering rescue efforts.
On Monday, the Houthi's military spokesperson Yahya Saree had reported the attack — without providing casualty figures — and vowed it would not go "unanswered."
Separate strikes on Monday killed 17 people and destroyed several buildings in the neighbouring coast province of Hodeida, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said.
CBS/AFP
3 oil tankers struck naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's navy says
The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that three oil tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, resulting in "explosions and massive fires."
There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.
On Saturday, three other oil tankers were hit in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.
CBS/AP
Top Iranian diplomat calls land blockade of Iran "impossible"

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called a land blockade of Iran "impossible" in comments shared Monday, according to Iranian state media. He also said pushing back against U.S. sanctions "is the duty of the entire country and its people," state media reported.
"The best way to counter this pressure is to make those imposing sanctions lose hope of achieving their goals, so they know this tool is ineffective and will remain so," Araghchi said.
Qatar's prime minister returns to Washington for Rubio meeting
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, in Washington, D.C., on Monday.

It was the Qatari official's second visit to Washington in recent weeks, after meeting with President Trump earlier this month. At the time, Mr. Trump had said he didn't see a reason to escalate the Iran war after the midterm elections.
Qatar has been a key mediator in indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran to end the conflict, which have stalled.
U.S. issues dozens of new sanctions against Iran

The U.S. Treasury Department issued new sanctions against a group of Iranian nationals and entities, which it described as front companies and exchange houses, on Monday. A list of two dozen names posted to its website included nine Iranian individuals in addition to businesses based, mainly, in Tehran and Dubai.

The Treasury said in a news release that the sanctions came as part of "a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks," which, according to the agency, allow billions to circulate internationally and "provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions."

"Iran's economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. "Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime. Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake."
Coalition fighting Houthis carried out hundreds of strikes in last few hours, Yemen says

The military coalition fighting Houthi rebels in Yemen carried out 647 strikes in the last few hours, the Yemeni government said Monday. The attacks included drone, rocket, field artillery and airstrikes, a government spokesperson said in a social media statement.

According to the spokesperson, those strikes "targeted militia positions, gatherings, fortifications and movements" and resulted in the "neutralization" of 122 Houthi commanders and members. More than 50 vehicles and pieces of military equipment were destroyed or disabled, the statement said.

In a separate statement, also shared to social media, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Saudi Air Force had carried out 67 airstrikes and missile attacks in the last 24 hours, and that dozens of civilians were killed or wounded.

Saree said the strikes killed and wounded dozens of civilians in targeted areas of Yemen's capital, Sana'a, as well as the governorates of Lahj, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada and Hajjah. But the Yemeni government blamed the Houthis for a missile attack Monday in Taiz, where, its spokesperson said, two civilians were killed and seven others were injured in the village of Kahlan.
Houthis say death toll from Saudi attack has risen to 17

Yemen's Houthi rebels said the death toll from a Saudi attack on the Red Sea port city of Hodeida rose to 17 Monday. The Iran-backed fighters, who control a massive portion of Yemen, including Hodeida, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognized government.

Coalition airstrikes on telecommunication facilities killed 17 workers, wounded 11 more and caused the "total destruction" of administrative buildings, staff housing, a mosque and other infrastructure on the compound, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said.
"This has led to the complete destruction of these facilities [and] the disruption of telecommunications and internet services," affecting tens of thousands of people, it said.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a social media post that another alleged Saudi coalition attack in the Lahj province, in Yemen's southwest, targeted buses and other vehicles. He said there were unspecified casualties.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on either of the purported attacks. The coalition said Sunday that it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched at Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast.
CBS/AFP
U.S. discussing training Syrian armed forces, Reuters reports

The United States is discussing plans to train Syrian soldiers to conduct demining work, five people familiar with the matter told the Reuters news agency. The plan could see a small number of U.S. troops return to Syria as soon as next year if it is adopted.

The proposal is for a multinational training mission – made up of 15 countries including the U.K., France and Saudi Arabia – to focus on demining and ordnance disposal. It would be the first time since 2024 that U.S. troops had trained Syrian counterparts.
The U.S. State Department told Reuters that Washington welcomed having a partner in the Syrian capital, , who is committed to combating the terror group ISIS.
U.S. officials would need to do due diligence to screen all prospective Syrian recipients of the training before any funding is dedicated to the prospective project, two of the sources told Reuters.
Iranian singer convicted of "outraging public decency" lashed 74 times for performing without hijab

An Iranian singer has been lashed 74 times after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without wearing the hijab head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.
Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed Monday over her 2024 live-streamed YouTube concert, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Etemad.

The lawyer told Etemad that Ahmadi and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom Monday as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
The criminal court in Qom upheld the convictions for "outraging public decency" citing "immoral" content posted online during Ahmadi's performance in December 2024, which went viral in Iran.
In addition to the 74 lashes, Parastoo and eight members of her team were also sentenced to a two-year ban on travel out of the country and a two-year ban on all "artistic activity."

Parastoo performed her concert in the Dayr-Gachin Caravanserai - an ancient site along the Silk Road route in Iran. It included themes of nationalism and popular uprising, and saw her openly flout both the Islamic Republic's dress code and a long-standing ban on women singing in public.
Netanyahu warns against downplaying "grave threats" facing Israel
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's now-caretaker prime minister, said Monday that Israel is still facing "serious and grave threats," and he warned of the dangers of downplaying them.

He spoke shortly after his domestic political opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, said he saw no immediate threat posed by Iran that would warrant military action before a new Israeli government is formed to oust Netanyahu.

"Anyone who belittles or downplays these immediate, serious and grave threats surrounding us does so for political reasons," Netanyahu said at a briefing in Israel's parliament, in which he called for a unity government, as Eisenkot attempts to form a new ruling coalition.
CBS/AFP
Netanyahu foe trying to form new Israeli government says no "immediate threat" requiring action against Iran

Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli politician trying to form a new government to oust current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the wake of national elections, has said he sees no "immediate threat" from Iran requiring military action.
Speaking at a meeting of his party, Yashar, Monday, he said: "I see no direct and immediate threat from Iran today that would require Israel to act before a new government is formed."
He added that "the gravest threat Iran poses" comes from its stockpile of enriched uranium: "That is where we need to focus."
Netanyahu has appeared keen to go on the offensive against Iran again. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News last week that Israel and the U.S. were .

Eisenkot recently said Netanyahu should not make any big national security decisions in the transition period following Israel's election, in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority, and that the now-caretaker prime minister should avoid "dangerous steps that can wait for the swearing in of a new government."
Iran seeks $290 billion in damages against the U.S.

Iran is due $290 billion from the United States to cover damages inflicted both during, and long before the war launched jointly by the U.S. and Israel almost nine months ago, Iran's judiciary authorities say.
Iranian courts have demanded the U.S. pay the sum, a judiciary official said Monday.

"We have secured court rulings in domestic courts awarding $290 billion in damages against the Americans," said Hassan Abdolianpour, head of the judiciary's center for lawyers, according to state television.
He also said several lawsuits had been filed against Persian Gulf Arab nations for "allowing their territory to be used by America to launch attacks against Iran."
According to state TV, the damages cover U.S. actions going back decades.

On Monday, state broadcaster IRIB said several U.S.-linked commercial ships had been seized and that part of the compensation owed to Iran would be settled through the seizures, without giving further details.
CBS/AFP
Lebanon denounces Israeli military official's visit to school in south
Lebanese officials have denounced a visit by an Israeli military spokesperson to a school in an Israeli-occupied area of southern Lebanon.

As Lebanon marked its independence day on Sunday, the Israeli military's Arabic-language spokesperson Ella Waweya shared a video on social media showing her outside a school in Debl, a Christian village, and then standing in front of a classroom full of children.

The village is located inside a wide swath of southern Lebanon that Israel has occupied and declared a "security zone" after the latest war erupted with Hezbollah in March. The zone covers a strip of southern Lebanon along the border and stretches about six miles into Lebanese territory.

Debl is among a number of Christian-majority villages near the border where many residents have refused to leave despite Israeli military orders to evacuate. Cut off from the rest of Lebanon, they are largely dependent on humanitarian aid.

"During my last visit to south Lebanon, I was amazed by the beauty of the land and the villages which have paid a heavy price due to their exploitation ... by a terrorist organization," Waweya said, referring to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam denounced Israel for "dragging students into a military and propaganda display."
"An occupying power has no right to exploit our children to embellish the image of its occupation or impose its dominance over our people in the south," he added.

Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March with rocket fire at Israel, which responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion. Lebanon says Israeli attacks since then have killed more than 4,300 people.
CBS/AFP
Iran says it will use "all available means" to counter U.S. blockade
Iran said Monday it would use all means at its disposal to counter a U.S. naval blockade imposed in retaliation for its own push to block the Strait of Hormuz.
"We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter U.S. aggression," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in his weekly press briefing.
Soon after the war broke out, the Strait of Hormuz became the focus of the conflict, with Iran continuing in its efforts to blockade the waterway, vital to global energy supplies.
In response, the U.S. imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports. It later announced a raft of economic sanctions, and launched a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran.

"You should bear in mind that what the Americans have described as economic sanctions, an economic blockade and a naval blockade undoubtedly constitutes an act of military aggression against Iran," said Baqaei. "Under these circumstances, Iran is entitled, pursuant to Article 51 of the U.N. Charter, to use any means at its disposal to defend itself."
Iran has said Hormuz could be open within two days but only if Washington agreed to its list of demands, which include the lifting of the blockade.
Houthi media say 4 dead in Saudi attack on key port city
Houthi media said Monday that a Saudi attack killed four people and wounded 18 in Yemen's key port city of Hodeida.
The Iran-backed fighters, who control large swathes of Yemen including Hodeida, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognized government.
The strike targeted a building belonging to Yemen's Public Telecommunications Corporation, the Houthis' Almasirah television channel wrote on X.
Riyadh didn't immediately comment on the report.
It came a day after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward the kingdom's western Red Sea coast.
That region is home to major oil installations that Houthi fighters have attacked in recent weeks, along with strikes on airports and military sites.
Yemen, which has been embroiled in more than a decade of civil war, was sucked into the U.S.-Iran conflict in July when a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government unraveled.
Since then, hostilities have left more than 1,600 people dead and more than 300,000 displaced in the country, the poorest on the Arabian Peninsula, according to the latest U.N. data.
Houthis say Saudi strike on Yemen capital wounds 6
Houthi rebels in Yemen reported an airstrike early Sunday in the capital, Sanaa.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, Anees al-Asbahi, said the strike hit a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company and wounded six workers.
The strike also damaged the company's building, al-Asbahi said.
The Red Sea port city of Mokha also came under fire on Sunday, Houthi-run television reported, as did the Haifan district in the southwestern province of Taiza.
The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the airstrikes but didn't report any casualties from them.
Trump says Iran launched more drones and missiles in past week "than at any time for over a year"

President Trump on Sunday acknowledged that Iran "has launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year," but he added: "Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage."
In a post on Truth Social, the president linked the midterm elections — in which in both chambers of Congress — to the escalation in the war with Iran.

"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections. One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred," Mr. Trump said.
Higher fuel prices triggered by the war caused economic concerns for Americans, and top Republicans, have partly attributed GOP election defeats to the war with Iran.
Mr. Trump on Sunday said voters "didn't understand" what their votes meant and called the election "very 'strange.'"

"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen! Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," he said. "Too bad the Voters didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger, but the whole Election was very 'strange.'"
Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to raise awareness of Iran war's toll on wildlife

British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.
Iran holds talks with Qatari mediators
Iranian deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran the previous evening and "held two hours of talks," without providing details.
Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran to end the war have stalled in recent months.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, however, that ongoing talks in the region must be "given a chance" and that the ongoing U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz "must be lifted rationally."
"Our position is clear: as long as Iran's demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless," he said, quoted by state television.
"At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves."
Iran's conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the U.S. counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
CBS/AFP
Trump says he wants to make "permanent" deal with Iranian regime
President Trump said Saturday that he wants to make a "permanent" deal with Iran that will prevent the country from gaining a nuclear weapon in the future.

"What I'm doing is I'm going to make it so that if we have an incompetent president in four years or 15 years or 20 years, I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent," Mr. Trump told Fox News in a phone interview on Saturday. "I'm not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon."

Mr. Trump said he's never "cared too much about the regime" leading Iran, and that he has "taken out two regimes already," though he declined to specify further. Former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the initial strikes on Iran that began the war in February 2026. His son Mojtaba Khamenei has held the title ever since.
Mr. Trump said Iranian officials have been "very, very difficult" to make a deal with.
"I mean, we make a deal and then they break the deal the next day," Mr. Trump said.

articles.headline: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
keyFacts: US Attorney General Todd Blanche called Nvidia a good corporate citizen while refusing to say if the company or its CEO is under investigation.
Lawmakers expressed anger over President Donald Trump helping reinstate Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang after his resignation over an alleged Chinese spy affair.
Huang is set to appear before Congress next week to answer questions regarding national security concerns and his relationship with an alleged spy.
body: - Published
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether it was being investigated by the administration.

Blanche said he had no information about Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement as the AI microchip maker's chief executive.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned over his relationship with a former executive for Megaspeed - the alleged China spy - due to national security concerns.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist tech company Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer that has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the expert investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen."

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that that the president is saying to the American people ... It shouldn't be what my message would be either," Blanche said.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price was down more than 7% in early afternoon trading, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's return was announced.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".
